title: Denmark Forgot Him. He Held the Fort.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Eskild Andersen Kongsbakke' (c.1620 Kungsbacka; commoner; joined the company 1639, sailed on the Christianshavn, arrived 1643; quartermaster under Leyel; chosen by soldiers and inhabitants after Korsør's death in 1655 because no Danish officers remained, almost illiterate; 1655 siege withstood with local support; a nine-month siege; town wall credited to him by Sethuraman, disputed by Bjørn Westerbeek Dahl; privateering against Mughal Bengal, trade with Bantam and Makassar; Denmark sceptical of his reports; Geert van Hagen sent 1668; Færø reached Tranquebar May 1669 with Henrik Eggers, who was to take over if Kongsbakke had died; villages of Poreiar, Tillali and Erikutanchery ceded; royal letter of 10 Dec 1670 reprimanded both men but reconfirmed Kongsbakke; quote 'That is the honor one gets for 5 years of service in Europe and 30 years in India'; Eggers sent to Copenhagen 1672 to explain himself; died at Dansborg c.1674; presumed Indian wife; Kay Larsen 1907 'the brave and loyal man who saved the fortress'; recent research less heroic, multicultural enclave)

Wikipedia, 'Sieges of Tranquebar (1655-1669)' (Vijaya Raghava needed money for campaigns against Gingee and Madurai; higher tribute demanded 1655; Christianshavn the last Danish ship for 26 years; 1648 mutiny, Leyel arrested; company dissolved 1650; Korsør died 7 September 1655; 1655 defence with local Indian and Portuguese mercenaries; 1660 siege of nine months; wall around the whole town and four new towers; before that only Dansborg fortified; peace in 1669)
Wikipedia, 'Danish India' (treaty with the Nayak of Tanjore, 20 November 1620, village granted for tribute; Tranquebar sold to Britain in 1845)
Wikipedia, 'Willem Leyel' and related pages (Christianshavn left Denmark 8 November 1639, delayed for years, reached Tranquebar September 1643)
Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Roskilde' (Halland, including Kungsbacka, ceded by Denmark to Sweden in 1658)

Danmarkshistorien (Aarhus University), 'Eskild Andersen Kongsbakke, ca. 1620-1674' (via search summary: instructions for the case that Kongsbakke had died and Tranquebar might no longer be Danish; Eggers found him alive, became vice-commander; van Hagen a Dutch sergeant from Negapatam)
Background: Rajiv Ahir, A Brief History of Modern India, 'The Danes'; National Museum of Denmark, 'Tranquebar: Danish era 1620-1845'

lines.text: Trang-keh-bar, southern India, sixteen sixty.
The king of Tan-jore's army has surrounded the town,
lines.caps: The king of Tanjore's *army | has *surrounded the town,

lines.text: and it will stay for nine months.
Inside the walls, the man in charge can barely read.
lines.caps: Inside the *walls, | the man in *charge | can barely *read.

lines.text: He has no orders, no money and no ships from home.
lines.caps: He has no *orders, | no *money | and no *ships from home.

lines.text: Denmark has forgotten him.
So why is he still flying its flag?
lines.caps: So *why is he | still flying its *flag?

lines.text: His name was Es-kil An-der-sen,
called Kongs-backa after his hometown,
then part of Denmark and now in Sweden.
lines.caps: then part of *Denmark | and now in *Sweden.

lines.text: He was a commoner, nobody important.
But he was stubborn, and that would matter.
lines.caps: But he was *stubborn, | and that would *matter.

lines.text: In sixteen thirty-nine he joined the Danish East India Company
lines.caps: In 1639 he *joined | the Danish East India *Company

lines.text: and sailed for its only fort in India,
lines.caps: and *sailed for | its only *fort in India,

lines.text: Dans-borg, at Trang-keh-bar.
The Danes rented the village from the Naa-yuk of Tan-jore,
lines.caps: The Danes *rented the village | from the Nayak of *Tanjore,

lines.text: in return for a yearly tribute.
But the voyage was so hard
that his ship, the Kris-chans-hown,
only reached India in sixteen forty-three.
Nobody aboard knew it yet,
but it would be the last Danish ship to arrive
lines.caps: but it would be | the *last Danish ship | to *arrive

lines.text: for twenty-six years.
But soon the colony began to fall apart.
lines.caps: But soon the *colony | began to fall *apart.

lines.text: In sixteen forty-eight, the garrison mutinied
and arrested its own governor.
Back home, Denmark was worn down by wars with Sweden,
lines.caps: *Back home, | Denmark was *worn down | by wars with *Sweden,

lines.text: so no ships could be spared.
Therefore, in sixteen fifty,
the bankrupt company was simply dissolved.
Trang-keh-bar was now an orphan:
a fort, a few soldiers,
and a rent bill nobody in Copenhagen meant to pay.
lines.caps: and a *rent bill | nobody in *Copenhagen | meant to *pay.

lines.text: Kongs-backa, now the fort's quartermaster,
did the one thing he could.
He made the soldiers stand guard and drill,
lines.caps: He made the *soldiers | stand guard and *drill,

lines.text: as if help were coming.
On the seventh of September, sixteen fifty-five,
the governor, Pole Han-sen Kor-sur, died.
No Danish officer was left to replace him.
lines.caps: No Danish *officer | was left to *replace him.

lines.text: So the soldiers and townspeople
chose the quartermaster.
An almost illiterate commoner
was now in charge of Denmark's only colony in India.
lines.caps: was now in *charge | of Denmark's *only colony | in *India.

lines.text: And almost at once, he had an enemy.
lines.caps: And *almost at once, | he had an *enemy.

lines.text: The Naa-yuk of Tan-jore, Vi-jaya Raa-gha-va,
needed money for his own wars against Jin-jee and Ma-doo-rai.
lines.caps: needed *money | for his own *wars | against Gingee and *Madurai.

lines.text: He saw a weak colony,
and he raised the rent.
Kongs-backa could not pay,
so the Naa-yuk sent an army.
But Kongs-backa had planned for this.
With Portuguese mercenaries and local Indian allies,
he held the fort, and the siege was lifted.
lines.caps: he *held the fort, | and the siege was *lifted.

lines.text: He knew the Naa-yuk would be back.
So he started building.
Until then, only the fort was defended.
When danger came, the townspeople crowded inside.
So Kongs-backa had a wall built around the whole town,
lines.caps: So Kongsbakke had a *wall | built *around | the whole *town,

lines.text: with new towers for cannon.
Historians still argue over how much of that wall was really his.
lines.caps: Historians still *argue | over how *much | of that *wall | was really *his.

lines.text: But when the Naa-yuk returned in sixteen sixty,
the siege lasted nine months,
and Trang-keh-bar still did not fall.
Holding a wall, though, costs money.
And he had none.
So the commander became a trader,
and sometimes a privateer.
He sent cargoes east to Ban-tam in Java,
lines.caps: He sent cargoes *east | to *Bantam in Java,

lines.text: and to Ma-kas-sar.
He waged a private war at sea
against the Mughal governor of Bengal,
seized his ships and sold their cargo.
The profits paid for soldiers and for repairs to Dans-borg.
lines.caps: The *profits paid for soldiers | and for *repairs | to *Dansborg.

lines.text: He sent hopeful reports home to Copenhagen.
Copenhagen did not believe them.
By sixteen sixty-eight, even Kongs-backa thought
the colony could not survive alone.
So he sent one last messenger,
a Dutchman named Hairt van Haagen,
all the way to Copenhagen.
This time, it worked.
In May sixteen sixty-nine,
a Danish frigate, the Fair-uh,
dropped anchor off Trang-keh-bar.
One of its officers, Hen-rik Eggers,
carried instructions for what to do
if Kongs-backa was dead and the town was lost.
lines.caps: if Kongsbakke was *dead | and the town was *lost.

lines.text: Instead, he found Kongs-backa alive,
and the colony in good order.
Peace with the Naa-yuk soon followed,
and it even gave the Danes new villages.
lines.caps: and it even *gave | the Danes new *villages.

lines.text: You might expect a hero's welcome.
He got the opposite.
Eggers and his officers looked down
on the commoner who could barely write,
and pushed him aside.
Kongs-backa complained bitterly:
that is the honour one gets
for five years of service in Europe,
and thirty years in India.
The king backed him, and called Eggers home.
lines.caps: The king *backed him, | and called Eggers *home.

lines.text: Kongs-backa stayed in command at Dans-borg
until he died, around sixteen seventy-four.
He never saw home again.
For a long time, Danish historians called him
lines.caps: For a *long time, | Danish *historians called him

lines.text: the loyal man who saved the colony.
Today, some argue the story is less simple.
lines.caps: Today, some *argue | the story is less *simple.

lines.text: Trang-keh-bar was a multicultural town,
he may have married an Indian woman,
and trading inside Asia may have paid better
lines.caps: and trading inside *Asia | may have paid *better

lines.text: than waiting for ships from Copenhagen.
Maybe that is the real lesson.
Kongs-backa did not survive because Denmark helped him.
lines.caps: *Kongsbakke did not survive | because *Denmark helped him.

lines.text: He survived because he stopped waiting for Denmark,
and became part of India.
And because he held on,
the Danish flag flew over Trang-keh-bar
for another hundred and seventy years.
